name: Chelation therapy
short: Deaths from low calcium on edetate disodium: a 5-year-old with autism; 2 children in a US report (diagnoses, overlap not given). Other children: Stevens-Johnson (DMPS); rash, less height (succimer).
text: Deaths and low blood calcium (case reports): a five-year-old autistic boy being given chelation in a physician's office went into cardiac arrest during his third treatment and died; only after his death was it found that he had been given edetate disodium rather than edetate calcium disodium, causing profound hypocalcaemia (low blood calcium), and the authors write that chelation in autistic children has not been validated and can have tragic consequences. A report to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention describes the deaths of 3 people from cardiac arrest caused by hypocalcaemia during chelation in 2003 to 2005; 2 were children, both treated with edetate disodium; the abstract does not give the children's diagnoses or say whether either was the boy above, and the adult case was still under investigation when it was written. A second report of three deaths associated with chelation-related hypocalcaemia that led to cardiac arrest, in Texas, Pennsylvania and Oregon in 2003 to 2005 (the abstract does not give the ages, diagnoses or chelating agent for these deaths), written about drugs used for lead poisoning, warns of the established risk of hypocalcaemia with edetate disodium and says it should not be given to children; neither abstract says whether the two reports describe the same deaths. Autism: a Cochrane review found one randomised placebo-controlled trial (repeated rounds of DMSA, dimercaptosuccinic acid, by mouth, in 49 children), found no clinical trial evidence that chelation is effective, cites prior reports of serious adverse events such as hypocalcaemia, kidney impairment and death, and concludes that the risks of chelation for autism currently outweigh proven benefits. A trial report in children with autism (65 children aged 3 to 8 given one round of DMSA by mouth, 49 then randomised; the abstract does not say whether this is the trial in the Cochrane review, whose first phase had 77 children) found some increase in urinary loss of essential minerals, especially potassium and chromium, and calls DMSA reasonably safe without giving adverse-event counts in the abstract. A commentary estimates that about half a million people with autism undergo chelation in the US each year and says unnecessary chelation can cause significant acute adverse effects and may have long-term consequences. Other children (mercury or lead exposure, not autism): an 11-year-old boy exposed to mercury vapour developed Stevens-Johnson syndrome (a severe blistering reaction of the skin and mouth) after two weeks of DMPS (dimercaptopropane sulfonate) by mouth, which resolved after it was stopped; the authors note that DMPS and DMSA are used in children with autism and are sold over the counter in some countries (a case report). In a placebo-controlled trial in 780 children aged 12 to 33 months with moderate blood lead levels, succimer (DMSA) by mouth led to more scalp rashes (3.5% versus 1.3%) and an unexpected excess of injuries, and children given succimer grew 0.43 cm less in height over 34 months than those given placebo. In a Nigerian programme of 3,180 courses of DMSA by mouth in children aged 5 or under with severe lead poisoning, moderate rises in the liver enzyme ALT occurred in under 2.5% of courses and no clinically severe adverse drug effects were seen; 20 children died during the period, with lead poisoning a primary factor in 6 (the abstract does not attribute any death to DMSA). An open-label study of 59 children aged 12 to 65 months found no adverse reactions attributable to DMSA. Adults (EDTA infusions after a heart attack, a different use): in a placebo-controlled trial of 40 intravenous infusions of a disodium EDTA-based solution in 1708 adults, the abstract reports similar numbers stopping infusions because of adverse events (38 with chelation, 41 with placebo) and no difference in total deaths (87 versus 93), although the trial was not powered for this comparison. Lyme disease: a review states that chelation given for nonconventional uses such as Lyme disease can cause significant adverse effects; no cited source studies chelation for Lyme disease or names the agent or route used for it, so the harms above, from edetate disodium, from oral DMSA and DMPS and from disodium EDTA infusions, may not describe it. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
